newsitem.title: SHARJAH: FEATURE - Sleepy Sharjah wakes up to cargo boom.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sleepy Sharjah wakes up to cargo boom.

text.p: Sofas, televisions, tyres and t-shirts are piled high in the warehouses waiting to be loaded onto lumbering old Russian aircraft parked in neat rows along the tarmac.
Across the way, state-of-the-art Lufthansa jumbos exchange cargoes with Singapore Airlines jets.
The UAE's oldest airport is buzzing as Sharjah -- Dubai's lower-profile, less-wealthy cousin just 30 km (20 miles) away -- quietly takes its place on the world air cargo map.
Last year it handled more than 320,000 tonnes of air freight -- up 19 percent on 1995. Dubai handled almost 360,000 tonnes.
Sharjah's figure is expected to double in the next few years as a new cargo terminal is built and more airlines are lured by promises of plenty of space, cheap rates and limited red tape.

"The growth is a good sign of economic development of the city and the infrastructure and airport facilities available. Airlines want to use these and they find them more economical," Sharjah airport general manager Ghanem al-Hajri told Reuters.
He said Sharjah is close to finalising plans to build a fourth cargo terminal and a new customs building, which should be on stream within a year.

The airport's cargo manager, Ibrahim Chehab, says space is the important thing. "We are very flexible, have a lot of space in our warehouse and huge parking for cargo aircraft. We are also cheaper than the others."
Airlines agree. "It's less crowded and the authority is quite accommodating and open minded," said one airline manager. The region is renowned for bureaucracy.
STILL OVERSHADOWED BY DUBAI

But until it can firmly establish a reputation as a central cargo hub strategically positioned mid-way between east and west, Sharjah will be overshadowed by Dubai's glitzy image and well-oiled marketing machine.

Lufthansa Cargo's arrival in 1993 marked a turning point for Sharjah, which first had an airstrip when a Royal Air Force base was set up in the 1930s. From 60 flights a month, the German carrier now operates about 300 flights through Sharjah.

Klaus Holler, Lufthansa hub manager, said the emirate's attraction in the early 1990s was its unused cargo terminal "which could be transformed in a relatively short period and the fact that they allowed us to do our own handling".
Clearly, there was a cost advantage too, Holler said.
Some analysts say landing in Sharjah is as much as five times cheaper than a busy European airport.

Last April Lufthansa Cargo India, a joint venture with India's Hinduja Group started operating four Boeing 727s to and from the Indian subcontinent. In November Lufthansa and Singapore Airlines started exchanging cargoes, an average 200 tonnes a week on each plane from Frankfurt and Singapore, at Sharjah.
Lufthansa is central to Sharjah attracting more airlines.
"We are marketing this hub concept and are talking to more airlines than before. Airlines usually follow each other and learn from each other," said Hajri.
IMPORTANCE OF CIS LINK

But the airport's bread and butter, albeit rather erratic, is the business from charter airlines from the former Soviet Union, most of which carry goods to CIS countries. Last year the most important destination for freight carried from Sharjah was Moscow. Tashkent and Baku were two other important destinations.

"I have been in the airline industry for 27 years, and I have never seen a range of Russian aircraft like they have here," said a British aircraft enthusiast visiting the airport to photograph the planes parked on the tarmac.
While old Russian aircraft face restrictions in many developed countries, Sharjah is more flexible.
"It is noisy, but we are far from the city and we hope for some improvement. But we have no restrictions," Hajri said.
He said that in the early days, getting used to dealing with some of the charter operators from the Commonwealth of Independent States was difficult.
"We took a risk early on. It was painful, even communication was difficult, but we helped them develop their operations and as time went by things improved remarkably."
Aeroflot is one of Sharjah's big operators, with almost 1,500 flight movements last year mostly on Ilyushin 76 and Ilyushin 86 and Tupolev-5 planes.
Afghanistan's Ariana Airlines is another key customer.
"It has two or three flights a day," said Chehab.

Last year Ariana recorded more than 1,500 flight movements. Much of its cargo -- mostly carried on Antonov 12s and Antonov 8s -- is destined for war-ravaged Kabul and varies from uniforms and boots to electronics sold in Dubai's downtown souks.
But it seems that Sharjah is destined to lure more of the sophisticated cargo carriers, with talk of some Asian heavyweights following Lufthansa's lead.
